POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSES TO REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1:
In this manuscript, Sharan et al. evaluate the impact of simultaneous initiation of cART and a three-month regimen of 3HP in a rhesus macaque model of LTBI with SIV co-infection. The primary outcomes of interest are immunologic, including CD4 T cell and CD8 T cell abundance in BAL and lung tissue and macrophage turnover. There are some exciting aspects of this study- in particular, this model offers bacteriologic and immunologic insights into a clinical intervention (addition of 3HP upon initiation of cART in individuals with LTBI) currently in clinical trials. However, there are significant limitations to the study that overall diminish my enthusiasm.
Response: Thank you for your insightful feedback on our manuscript. We appreciate your positive comments on the exciting aspects of the study, especially in terms of providing both bacteriologic and immunologic insights into the clinical intervention of adding 3HP upon initiation of cART in individuals with LTBI. We have now provided more detailed explanations and context regarding these limitations in both the Discussion and the Methods sections to ensure the study's findings are appropriately framed. We hope that the revisions will address your concerns, making the study more robust and informative. Thank you again for your constructive critique.
Major comments:
1. Limited scope of new investigations: As transparently acknowledged by the authors in the text of the manuscript, many of the experimental results of this work were part of their previous work/have previously been published. This includes all of the immunologic comparisons of BAL and tissue T cells and macrophages in RMs with LTBI and SIV co-infection who do or do not receive cART. The new experimental condition introduced in this work is the addition of 3HP upon initiation of cART. There are some differences in that experimental group noted in the BAL T cells, including activated T cells, and some differences in cytokines in 3HP-treated RMs. However, it’s not entirely clear what the significance of these differences are for reactivation of any remaining viable Mtb or what the significance is in terms of future immunologic protection from reinfection. The overall insights gleaned from the work are limited, and this seems to be reflected in the abstract and discussion- reading them both carefully, it’s hard to pin down what the most significant or impactful findings are in the work.
Response: The authors thank the reviewer for their feedback. Modeling antiretroviral therapy (ART) and anti-tuberculosis (anti-TB) therapy in M. tuberculosis (Mtb) and HIV co-infection in nonhuman primates (NHPs) is crucial from a human perspective because it provides a more accurate representation of the complex interactions between these two infections, which is challenging to fully replicate in human clinical studies. NHPs, particularly rhesus macaques, are genetically similar to humans and offer a unique opportunity to study the immune and microbiological responses to co-infection in a controlled environment. This model allows for the evaluation of therapeutic strategies such as the simultaneous initiation of ART and anti-TB treatment, which is currently being tested in clinical trials for individuals with latent TB and HIV co-infection. Understanding the pulmonary immune responses pre-and post-therapy, and potential drug interactions in NHPs provides critical insights into the unique challenges posed by HIV co-infection. Moreover, NHP models are essential for exploring the safety, efficacy, and timing of combined therapies, ultimately leading to better clinical outcomes in people living with both HIV and TB. Although the WHO recommends concurrent 3HP and cART in TB-endemic settings, uptake remains poor and the immune mechanisms underlying the benefits of concurrent cART and 3HP have not been defined. Identifying the components of TB immunity that remain impaired after ART, versus those that are restored by concurrent ART and 3HP is an innovative approach to identify correlates of immune control versus reactivation. Such studies will also aid in targeting potential targets for host-directed therapies that further improve treatment regimens for TB/HIV and provide insights into designing therapeutic vaccines that prevent reactivation of LTBI.
Lines 398-413.
In this manuscript, we used historical controls to minimize the numbers of animals used, consistent with standard practices in NHP research encouraging the use of archived samples or control cohorts to reduce the number of study animals for repeated measures of same readouts. We wanted to compare the T , T , immune activation H1 H17 markers that were reconstituted in cART+3HP groups compared to cART only and cART naïve group and to ascertain if the reconstitution was comparable to the immune responses seen in LTBI. Hence, we chose to use previously completed cohorts. We determined that concurrent treatment of Mtb/SIV co-infected rhesus macaques with cART and 3HP did not rescue the immune defect (initiated as early as the first 2 weeks of SIV co-infection) better than cART alone. Specifically, cART+3HP did not control virus-driven chronic immune activation in the pulmonary compartment (HLA-DR+CD4+ T and CD69+CD4+ T cells), or periphery (CXCR3+CCR6+CD4+ T cells). Additionally, the global frequency of CD4+ T cell as well as the Mtb-specific CD4+ effector memory T cells remained significantly lower at the end of cART and cART+3HP treatment compared to LTBI only macaques demonstrating failure of treatment to reconstitute the functional responses in the pulmonary compartment. These are critical novel findings in a biologically relevant preclinical animal model and has important clinical implications for humans who receive these treatments. Lines 417-431.
The main finding of this study is the incomplete immune reconstitution and persistent immune-mediated inflammation, even with LTBI treatment and concomitant cART. This is a crucial finding and we believe it underscores the complexity of TB and HIV co-infection, particularly in the context of treatment. While cART+3HP clearly provides benefits, our findings highlight the persistent challenges in eliminating inflammation, which may continue to hinder TB responses despite the intervention. Lines 452-456.
2. Limited information offered from the scRNAseq analysis: scRNAseq analysis can potentially offer substantial insight, in particular into subpopulation shifts under different conditions and the dominant expression modules in those subpopulations. Two of the six figures in the paper are devoted to scRNAseq- a substantial proportion of the paper. However, the scRNAseq analysis offered here provides minimal complementary insight into immune dynamics during treatment. There’s no text description of a key takeaway from Figure 5D aside from the number of clusters identified, and 5E and 5F seem to provide no interpretable information at all. Figure 6 is slightly more interpretable, but it’s still hard to find a clear takeaway from the data.
Response: We introduced significant changes to how scRNAseq data was analyzed and interpreted. As senior author, Dr. Kaushal recruited Dr. Hulin Wu, Professor and Director of Biostatistics at University of Texas Health Sciences Center at Houston, and his team of bioinformaticians/biostatisticians. We have now significantly revised both the Figures. Figure 5 includes the study design, tSNE plot representing the clusters, feature plots of selected genes representing annotation, and plots representing the cell counts per cluster per time point. We identified eight clusters in the BAL collected at weeks 5, week 11, week 13 and necropsy; macrophages, monocytes, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, Basophils, NK/NKT cells and mast cells. scRNAseq data validates our previous findings of a significant reduction in CD4+ T cell counts and proportions post SIV co-infection that cART+3HP does not restore to levels seen in LTBI. Newer analyses further inform us about the dynamics of other immunocytes critical to TB immunity, that we did not study using the traditional flow cytometry technique: macrophages, monocytes, NK/NKT cells and mast cells (Figure 5F-5J, Supplementary Figure 8).
Figure 6A includes Violin plots displaying the distributions of 42 differentially expressed genes across cell clusters (color-coded) when comparing three time points (week 5, week 11, and necropsy). These genes were associated with TH1 (IFNG, IFNGR1, IFNGR2, TBX21, STAT1, TNFAIP2, TNFAIP3, TNFAIP8, TNFAIP8L1, TNFAIP8L3, IL2, IL2RA, and BHLHE40), TH17 (IL20, IL20RA, IL20RB, IL21, IL21R, IL22, IL22RA1, IL22RA2, IL23A, IL23R, RORA, and STAT3), and immune activation (IDO-1, IRF4, CD38, CD69, LAG3, ICOS, CTLA4, IL13, CXCL10, CXCR1, CXCL12, CXCL13, IL27, KLRD1, IL6, MMP9, and FCGR1A). As shown in Figure 6A and 6B, there was a significant difference in DGE in macrophage, monocyte and CD8+ T cell clusters.
Only genes with a raw p-value < 0.05 and a log2 fold change > 1 were retained for subsequent Gene Ontology (GO) (Figure 6C) and GSEA pathway enrichment analyses (Figure 6D). In these analyses, enriched terms were defined as those with a FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) corrected p-value < 0.05 and a Storey’s q-value < 0.05. All enrichment analyses were performed using the Bioconductor package clusterProfiler. The GO enriched pathways include response to type I interferon, interferon-mediated signaling pathway, cellular response to type I interferon and activation of the innate immune response. The GSEA enriched pathways include cytokine mediated signaling pathway, response to type I interferon and innate immune response.
Lastly, In Figure 6E and 6F, we have now included the ridge plots from the scRNAseq showing expression levels of genes associated with immune activation; CD38 and CD69. We report an increased immune activation-associated CD38 and CD69 gene expression in both lymphoid and myeloid clusters.
In conclusion, the activation of innate immune pathways, particularly those related to type I interferon responses, plays a crucial role in the immune dynamics of TB/HIV co-infection. The differential expression of genes associated with T and T responses, as well as immune activation markers, underscores the complexity of the immune response during co-infection. Importantly, the enrichment of pathways related to type I interferon and innate immunity highlights the significance of these pathways in modulating the host's defense against both tuberculosis and HIV. Understanding how these immune responses evolve over time could provide valuable insights into potential therapeutic strategies for managing TB/HIV co-infection (Lines 376-382).

Reviewer #2:
In this manuscript, Sharan et. al. examine the impact of concurrent cART and Isoniazid and Rifapentine (3HP) treatment during MtB and SIV co-infection in a NHP model. Following 12 weeks of combined treatment cART+3HP animals demonstrate decreased bacterial burden. Despite this significant and promising finding, the authors report incomplete immune reconstitution and continued evidence for immune exhaustion and inflammation. These findings expand upon the groups previous findings and use historical data for comparison to their cART+3HP contemporary cohort. Although the results presented are of interest, there are gaps in the methodology and data that, in its current state, limit the data interpretation.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment of our study and the recognition of the promising findings regarding the impact of concurrent cART and 3HP treatment in the context of Mtb and SIV co-infection in a non-human primate (NHP) model.
We recognize that some aspects of our study design and data collection may not have been fully explained in the initial manuscript. In particular, we have provided more detailed descriptions of the study cohorts (Revised Figure 1A), the treatment protocols, and the timing of key measurements (e.g., bacterial burden, immune reconstitution, and inflammation markers) Lines 109-128. Additionally, we have expanded on the rationale for using historical data for comparison with the cART+3HP cohort (Lines 417-431) and clarified the methodological approach to ensure that these comparisons are robust (Lines 585-591, 618-620, 626-633, 648-653, 658-661, 668-675, 694-710; 715-723).
Major Comments:
1. Historical data from animals enrolled in the LTBI, cART naïve, and cART group were used as comparators for the experimental cART+3HP group. While leveraging historical samples is important for reducing the number of NHPs enrolled in the study, it is a limitation of the study. Additional scrutiny and information is needed to confirm the validity and rigor of the findings:
a. Prior to the start of the combined treatment regimen (Week 11) how comparable are the clinical disease and bacterial burden between the cART+3HP and historical groups used for comparison? Lines 532-533 indicate that “Bacterial burden in BAL was measured throughout the study”, please provide this data in comparison to historical groups.
Response: The authors thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. In response, we have now included the BAL CFU counts from each individual macaque per group at pre-infection and at weeks 3, 5, and 7 post-Mtb infection (Supplementary Figure 1C). This addition ensures a comprehensive comparison of CFU data throughout the latent phase of the experiment. Based on our previous studies, we have consistently observed stable latent CFU across all experiments conducted to date with no significant difference between study cohorts for this parameter. Line 119-120.
b. How do animal demographics (Supplemental Table 2) influence the interpretation of the results? e.g. age, sex, MHC class. Sex differences are inadequately addressed. The cART naïve and LTBI groups are exclusively male, cART+3HP is mostly male and cART treated is mostly female.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the influence of animal demographics, particularly sex and MHC class, on the interpretation of our results. We recognize that demographic factors can potentially affect the outcomes of studies and the generalizability of findings. However, given that the primary focus of this study is not specifically sex differences, we think that while sex may influence certain aspects of the immune response, the main conclusions of the study remain valid. Sex differences are difficult to study in the NHP model. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, an already existing shortage of research macaques in the Western world has been exacerbated, limiting the choices available to research groups like ours. Nonetheless, we emphasize the need for further research to explore how sex differences interact with treatment regimens in similar models. Lines 533-537.
2. Details regarding necropsy need to be clear and consistent.
a. Based on Supplemental Figure 2C, necropsies between the groups appear to occur at different timepoints (LTBI Wk23-25), cART naïve (Wk17-23), cART (Wk19-20) and cART+3HP (Wk23-24). How might bacterial burden or immune responses differ between these varying timepoints?
Response: We thank the reviewer for their feedback. We agree that the differences in necropsy timepoints across the groups could potentially influence bacterial burden and immune responses. However, all four groups were euthanized before week 24, which was the consistent humane endpoint determined in consultation with the veterinarians. We appreciate the concern regarding the varying time points, and we believe the observed differences in bacterial burden and immune responses can be explained by the mechanisms underlying each group’s treatment protocol. As expected, the bacterial burden in the LTBI and cART+3HP groups were comparable, given that both rely on distinct mechanisms for bacterial control (host control in the LTBI group and drug control in the cART+3HP group). In contrast, the cART naïve animals demonstrated a higher bacterial burden with extrapulmonary spread, consistent with LTBI reactivation and dissemination upon SIV co-infection. The bacterial burden in the cART-only group is also as expected, given the absence of anti-TB therapy. As we have previously shown, cART alone does not result in bacterial control (PMID: 34855621). Regarding immune responses, they differed across the four groups, as described in Figures 2-4. We do not think the differences were due to necropsy time points but due to the different conditions of treatment in these four cohorts. However, there were some comparable observations, including an expansion of the central memory response in both CD4 and CD8 T cells in both cART and cART+3HP groups. Additionally, we observed partial reconstitution of CD4 T cells and increased immune activation, exhaustion, and inflammation in the cART naïve, cART, and cART+3HP groups compared to the LTBI group. These findings are consistent with what we would expect from the immune dynamics in these cohort based on the treatment. Lines 437-443.
b. What were the humane endpoints used (Lines 128-129)? If some of the necropsies were planned as a study endpoints then the survival data in Supplemental Figure 2C is misleading.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s comment and have now added details on the necropsy time points in the Methods section “Animal infection” at Lines 585-591 to reflect the specific details of necropsy time points per group. Additionally, we have provided the explanation in text to better contextualize the necropsy details with the manuscript findings, Lines 124-127.
c. Necropsy timepoints are inconsistently described and the timing is critical for data interpretation. 1) Line 129 indicates some animals were euthanized “2 weeks post SIV co-infection”, which according to Figure 1A would correspond to Wk11, yet the Supplemental Figure 1C indicates Week 17 as the earliest necropsy. 2) Lines 507-509 indicate that “All the RMS in the cART-naïve group had to be euthanized within 2-4 weeks of cART treatment”, which according to Figure 1A would correspond to Wks13-15, yet the Supplemental Figure 1C indicates Week 17-23 as the necropsy timepoints. 3) Lines 509-510 “the RMs incART+3HP group were euthanized at end of 12-week treatment at week 24,” but Figure 1 C shows that 1 animal went to necropsy at Week 23.
Response: The authors have now revised the methods section “Animal infection” at Lines 585-591 to reflect the specific details of necropsy time points per group. The RMs in LTBI control group were euthanized at week 24 post Mtb infection. All the RMs in cART-naive group were euthanized between 17-24 weeks post Mtb infection due to clinical signs of LTBI reactivation. The RMs in the cART group were euthanized after 9 weeks of cART treatment or at week 20 post Mtb infection while the RMs in cART+3HP group were euthanized at end of 12-week treatment or at week 24 post Mtb infection. All animals were euthanized by week 24, which was the predetermined study endpoint, or at earlier time points if they became clinically unwell and/or showed signs of TB reactivation, as assessed by veterinarians in accordance with humane endpoint criteria.
3. In the current submission, an insufficient amount of details is provided for the experiments to be reproduced.
a. Details of how samples were collected, processed, and/or stored prior to analysis should be provided.
1)Immune responses in Figures 2 and 3 between the BAL and lung are not consistent. Why might this be?
Response: The authors have provided the total BAL CD4 (Fig. 2A) and Lung CD4 (Fig. 2B) and total BAL CD8 (Fig. 2C) and Lung CD8 T (Fig. 2D) cell percentage in Figure 2. Figure 3 represents CD4+ T and CD8+T cell subsets – CD4+ T central memory response and CD4+T effector memory response in the BAL and lung. Further Figure 2 represents markers of immune activation, exhaustion, trafficking and T * phenotype while Figure 3 represents the longitudinal changes in central and effector response of CD4 and CD8 in BAL (Fig. 3A-D) and comparison of central and effector memory response at necropsy between cART only and cART+3HP groups in BAL and lung (Fig. 3E-L). Hence there are 2 different sets of data presented in Figures 2 and 3.
2) In Figure 4 how were cells processed and stored before being thawed for the single cell experimentation?
Response: The authors have now added the BAL cell isolation protocol at Lines 668-675. BAL was performed with 80 mL of sterile saline in BSL3 on NHPs at weeks 5, 11 and necropsy after Mtb infection. The BAL was filtered, centrifuged (1,200 rpm, 10 min at 4C), lysed for red blood cells (RBCs) using ACK lysis buffer (GibcoTM) and resuspended in 2 mL final volume of RPMI 1640 media (GibcoTM). The cells were counted and live cells were used to perform ex-vivo antigen stimulation to measure Mtb-specific response. The prepared single cells were stained for surface and intracellular markers to study various cell phenotypes. The freshly collected BAL cells were stimulated ex vivo with Mtb-specific antigen, ESAT-6/CFP-10 (BEI Resources, 10 μg/mL), for a total of 16 hours. Brefeldin A (0.5 μg/mL, Sigma-Aldrich) was added 2 hours after the onset of stimulation. Additionally, the cells were counted and frozen in Cryostor in internally threaded cryovials in liquid nitrogen for downstream scRNA-seq processing using 10x Genomics platform. The BAL cells were frozen in Cryostor (Sigma Aldrich). Cryostor is formulated to contain 2% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Cryostor is designed to preserve the cell viability and functionality through modulation of cellular biochemical response to the cryopreservation process. Our lab routinely utilizes this reagent to preserve freshly isolated BAL cells.
b. What statistical tests were used for Figure 1B and G. In Figure 1B what is being compared?
Response: The authors have added the statistical tests used for Figure 1B and 1G (now supplementary Figure 1D) in the Figure legend (Lines 1002-1004, Line 1102). Nonparametric Mann-Whitney 2-tailed Student’s t test was used to compare 2 groups at individual time points in Figure 1B. Specifically, cART naïve group RMs were compared with cART+3HP RMs at weeks 13, 15 and 17. cART only group RMs are also compared with cART+3HP group RMs at weeks 13, 15 and 17. CRP levels in RMs in the cART+3HP group were significantly lower than in the cART-treated RMs (P < 0.001) at weeks 13 (P < 0.001), 15 (P < 0.0001) and 17 post Mtb infection (P < 0.0001) (Figure 1B). Nonparametric Mann-Whitney 2-tailed Student’s t test was used to compare plasma viral loads in cART only group RMs and cART+3HP at weeks 13, 15 and necropsy (Supplementary Figure 1D). No significant difference was observed in the plasma viral groups indicating comparable levels of viral control in both the groups.
c. The method details and flow cytometry panel used in Figure 2 should be provided.
Response: The authors have provided method details of lung tissue and BAL processing as well as the flow cytometry protocol used at Lines 626-633. The panel used has been provided in Supplementary Table 5.
d. Line 115: As the LTBI group did not receive SIV, this statement is incorrect.
Response: The authors thank the reviewer for the correction. The statement is now corrected at Line 114.
e. The gating scheme in Supplemental Figure 2 identifies Tem as CD28- CD95-, but are defined correctly by the authors as CD28-CD95+. Please explain this discrepancy.
Response: The revised visual representation of the gates has been added to reflect the gating strategy used to analyze the data (Tem is defined as CD28-CD95+) in Supplementary Figure 2.

Response: The authors thank the reviewer for pointing this out. Indeed, 24 samples were used for all the analysis (BAL samples were taken from six rhesus macaques at four time points = 24 samples). This has been corrected in both methods (Line 694, 1093, 128, 135, 144, 158).

Reviewer #3:
This is a well-executed study that combines several investigative modalities to demonstrate the effect of concurrent TB (3HP) therapy and HIV ART (emtricitabine/tenofovir/dolutegravir) in a non-human primate model of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) and simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) co-infection. Using techniques such as histopathology/immunohistochemistry, PET/CT, flow cytometry, RNA sequencing, and ELISA, these authors demonstrate novel insights into immune reconstitution and persistent inflammation in the lungs despite viral and bacterial control with combination therapy.
Response: Thank you for the positive feedback. We appreciate your recognition of the combination of investigative techniques we used to explore the effects of concurrent TB therapy (3HP) and cART in the non-human primate model of Mtb and SIV co-infection. We’re glad that our findings on immune reconstitution and persistent inflammation despite viral and bacterial control were insightful and valuable to you. Thank you again for your thoughtful comments.
Overall, they demonstrated that ART+3HP certainly reduced the burden of pulmonary TB burden at study endpoint compared to cart alone and untreated animals. TH1/TH17 CD4 T cel responses also increased in ART+3HP treated animals but incomplete immune reconstitution and persistent immune-mediated inflammation persisted regardless of LTBI txt and concomitant ART. Overall, this is an interesting finding that suggests that in the setting of SIV (and perhaps HIV) initiation of ART with 3HP certainly has benefits but does not eliminate TB (or HIV) associated inflammation which can hinder TB responses.
Response: We also acknowledge your observation regarding the incomplete immune reconstitution and persistent immune-mediated inflammation, even with LTBI treatment and concomitant ART. This is a crucial point, and we believe it underscores the complexity of TB and HIV co-infection, particularly in the context of SIV. While ART+3HP clearly provides benefits, our findings highlight the persistent challenges in eliminating inflammation, which may continue to hinder TB responses despite the intervention.
One general comment is how the TB infection model adequately recapitulates LTBI in the human population, especially those in endemic areas with multiple long-term exposures. I realize there are limitations to all animals models of LTBI, but some discussion on this and addressing how LTBI in the macaque differ from human LTBI would be essential in understanding and extrapolating these results.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the relevance of our macaque model in recapitulating latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in humans, particularly in individuals from endemic areas with multiple long-term exposures. We acknowledge the limitations inherent in animal models of LTBI, and we agree that it is crucial to highlight the distinctions between macaque models and human LTBI to properly contextualize our findings.
In response to this, we have revised the manuscript to include a more thorough discussion of the differences between LTBI in macaques and humans. Specifically, we emphasize that while macaques exhibit a form of LTBI that shares key characteristics with human infection—such as the persistence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a non-replicating state—there are notable differences. For example, macaques tend to develop a more robust immune response compared to humans, potentially leading to differences in the dynamics of infection and latency. Furthermore, the frequency of multiple, chronic exposures in endemic human populations may differ from the controlled exposures in macaque models, which could affect the progression and persistence of the infection. While the macaque model provides valuable insights, we recognize the need for careful extrapolation when translating these findings to human LTBI, particularly in highly endemic regions. Thank you again for this constructive feedback, which has helped strengthen our manuscript. Lines 533-552.
With particular regard to the imaging component of this study, FDG PET/CT scans were used to study lung lesions in a subset of the rhesus macaque subjects at certain timepoints: Week 6 (LTBI phase), Week 12 (1 week post cART+3HP initiation), Week 16 (4 weeks post cART+3HP initiation), and Week 22 (10 weeks post cART+3HP initiation). The authors used the lack of lung lesion progression at week 6 to demonstrate an LTBI state, which as above, is questionable to how this equates to LTBI in humans. For example, a suspicion lesion with any evidence of mTB on BAL, sputum culture or gene applification would be considered active TB. Further clarification of how stability of lesions equates to LTBI should be povided.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback regarding the interpretation of lung lesion stability in the context of LTBI.
In our study, FDG PET/CT imaging was used to monitor lung lesions in rhesus macaque subjects at several time points, including Week 6 (LTBI phase), Week 9 (LTBI+SIV), Week 12 (LTBI+SIV+cART+3HP), and Week 23 (End of cART+3HP treatment) (Revised Figure 1I). At Week 6, we observed no progression of lung lesions, which was interpreted as evidence of a stable, LTBI-like state. However, we acknowledge that the absence of lesion progression alone does not equate to a definitive diagnosis of LTBI, particularly given the complex nature of TB diagnosis in humans.
To address this, we incorporated additional diagnostic measures to confirm LTBI in our study. Infection was confirmed through a positive tuberculin skin test (TST) at weeks 3 and 5 post Mtb infection. All study RMs developed LTBI, which was characterized by serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels of 5 µg/mL or lower (Figure 1B), no significant changes in body temperature (Supplemental Figure 1A) or body weight (Supplemental Figure 1B) up to 9 weeks post-Mtb infection, and less than 1 to 2 Log10 CFU of Mtb in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) at weeks 3, 5, and 7 post-infection (Supplementary Figure 1C). Lines 109-127.
Additionally, we measured Mtb-specific immune responses by isolating BAL cells at week 5 post-low-dose Mtb infection. These cells were stimulated ex vivo with ESAT-6/CFP-10 antigens, and cytokine responses (IFN-g, IL-2, IL-17, and TNF-a) were measured to assess Mtb-specific response in the pulmonary compartment of macaques during the LTBI phase of the study.
In response to the reviewer’s concern, we have now clarified in the manuscript that the stability of lung lesions at Week 6, while suggestive of LTBI, was corroborated with these other diagnostic parameters (TST, CRP levels, immune responses, and bacterial load) that together support the LTBI diagnosis in this macaque model. Lines 116-120. We recognize that more comprehensive microbiological testing and longer follow-up would be required to confirm a definitive LTBI diagnosis in both non-human primates and humans.
At week 12, a significant increase in 18F-FDG uptake in the lungs was ascribed to progression of TB pathology in the setting of SIV co-infection. Following therapy with ART and 3HP, there was no progression of the size of the lung lesions, however metabolic activity by PET did not decrease. The authors suggest that combination treatment aided in treatment of caseous lesions but did not reduce the ongoing inflammation in the lungs.
Overall, the use of PET/CT in this study is a strength which serves to supplement the researchers’ other investigative modalities, offering a longitudinal visual element. Further, the use of both CT and PET helps to demonstrate both structural changes as well as metabolic activity. It is interesting to note that the lesions that did persist on ART+3HP remained PET avid, suggesting ongoing increase metabolic processes in these lesions, which, in some ways, would be expected if 3HP and ART railed to fully suppress or eradicate these lesions. One wonders, however, given the limitations of understanding how this LTBI model holes up to human disease, if these foci represent undertreated active TB rather than failure to control inflammation or immune responses in “latent” associated lesions. It seems from images and from other direct lung data that the “LTBI” here is more on the end of mild active TB disease. Further discussion on this would significantly strengthen the paper. E.g. would actually treating the monkey with at least 2 active drugs for a full treatment course result in different outcomes- one would assume so given the data presented.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the interpretation of the PET/CT imaging data. We acknowledge the reviewer’s comment about the persistence of PET-avid lesions during the cART and 3HP treatment period, despite no significant progression in lesion size. This observation suggests that while combination therapy with cART and 3HP might have reduced the caseous components of the lesions, it did not fully suppress the ongoing metabolic activity, which can be interpreted as indicative of persistent inflammation in these lesions.
As noted by the reviewer, the continued metabolic activity within the lesions could be interpreted in different ways. While we suggested that this might reflect ongoing inflammation rather than active bacterial replication, we agree that the presence of PET-avid lesions despite therapy may also raise the possibility of undertreated active TB, rather than a true LTBI state. The distinction between “mild active TB” and “latent” TB is indeed a nuanced one, and as the reviewer points out, our macaque model may better represent a transitional state between active and latent TB, rather than fully quiescent LTBI as understood in humans. Lines 180-188.
In response to this suggestion, we have revised the manuscript to discuss this issue more thoroughly.
Specifically, we highlight that while the macaque model is an important tool for studying LTBI, its precise equivalence to human disease remains uncertain. The persistence of PET-avid lesions despite the initiation of ART and 3HP treatment raises valid questions about the ability of these therapies to fully suppress infection in this model. As the reviewer suggests, it is possible that a more aggressive treatment regimen, including at least two active drugs over a full treatment course, could lead to different outcomes in terms of lesion resolution and metabolic activity. Lines 180-188
We have added this discussion to the manuscript, proposing that future studies could explore the effects of more intensive anti-TB therapy on the resolution of both lesion size and metabolic activity in this model. This would help determine whether the observed lesions represent a failure of immune control or are indeed indicative of undertreated active TB, providing further insight into the transition between active and latent TB. Lines Lines 180-188.
We believe these revisions strengthen the manuscript by addressing the complexities of interpreting PET/CT data in the context of TB therapy and LTBI, as well as emphasizing the need for further investigation into the best treatment strategies for LTBI in non-human primates.
Areas in which this study could be improved include sample size and lack of an ART-only control group. The small sample size of 3 macaques for the imaging component of the study carries a limitation in power with the understanding that these are expensive and logistically difficult studies. The lack of a 3HP control arm also makes it somewhat difficult to know the full extent of 3HP on TB infection.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. The authors would like to clarify that we do have a cART only control group (n = 4) (PMID: 34855621) that we included in this study. Additionally, we have published impact of 3HP on low dose TB infection previously (PMID: 35862216). A once-weekly oral dose of isoniazid and rifapentine for 3 months (3HP) is recommended by the CDC for treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI). The aim of this study was to assess 3HP-mediated clearance of M. tuberculosis bacteria in macaques with asymptomatic LTBI. Twelve Indian-origin rhesus macaques were infected with a low dose (~10 CFU) of M. tuberculosis CDC1551 via aerosol. Six animals were treated with 3HP and 6 were left untreated. The animals were imaged via PET/CT at frequent intervals. Upon treatment completion, all animals except 1 were coinfected with SIV to assess reactivation of LTBI to active tuberculosis (ATB). Four of 6 treated macaques showed no evidence of persistent bacilli or extrapulmonary spread until the study end point. PET/CT demonstrated the presence of significantly more granulomas in untreated animals relative to the treated group. The untreated animals harbored persistent bacilli and demonstrated tuberculosis (TB) reactivation following SIV coinfection, while none of the treated animals reactivated to ATB. 3HP treatment effectively reduced persistent infection with M. tuberculosis but did not sterilize the bacteria. This has implications of individuals in TB-endemic countries who are potentially still susceptible to TB infection or reactivation.

Given the high cost and logistical challenges associated with conducting imaging studies in non-human primates, including the time, resources, and specialized expertise required for such experiments, we were constrained by the number of macaques that could be included. However, despite this limitation, we believe the findings provide valuable preliminary insights into [the topic of study], and we hope that this work will lay the foundation for future studies with larger sample sizes. We have noted this limitation in the revised manuscript and discussed it as a point for consideration in future research directions Lines 545-552.

E.g. it is often difficult to know what each RM group refers to in the text or which group underwent which therapy or had which outcome. The figures are much clearer.

Reviewer #5:
Brief summary of findings:
The manuscript by Sharan et. al. examines the effect of combined TB and HIV therapies in a rhesus macaque model for latent TB infection (LTBI) and Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) co-infection. The authors studied the effect of cART and isoniazid and rifapentine (3HP) treatment in the coinfected animals on the components of TB immunity in lung, control of bacterial infection and clinical presentation of TB compared to coinfected animals with or without cART and untreated LTBI animals. Although the combination treatment showed lower levels of bacterial infection compared to other conditions, CD4+ T cells were not fully restored and the reconstituted CD4+ T cells also showed activated, exhausted and inflamed phenotype. Additionally, enrichment of Type 1 interferon related transcriptional signature and TB specific TH1/TH17 responses were seen but TB specific TNFa was reduced in the combination treatment. Overall, the study showed that combination cART and 3HP treatment in itself was not sufficient to prevent activation of TB because of certain immune mechanisms in the lung compartment.
Overall assessment of quality and importance:
The study addresses an important issue of latent TB activation in the context of HIV infection and seeks to examine if combination of cART and 3HP would be effective in preventing progression of TB in an in vivo model. The results showing reduction of bacteria after the combination treatment were quite promising. Data showing suboptimal reconstitution of immune cells in the lungs although disappointing are informative in guiding future studies on treating concurrent HIV and activation of latent TB. The experiments are well designed with sufficient numbers of replicates for each condition and the methods are well-suited to the questions being asked. The interpretations of results are generally reasonable and the manuscript is easy to read. The use of transcriptomic methods to understand what biological mechanisms might be impairing immune function is justified. However, this reviewer has major concerns about how the transcriptomic data (especially from single-cell sequencing) are presented and interpreted in the manuscript. This part of the paper requires significant improvement before being ready for publication. Specific concerns are described below.

Response: We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the improvements in contextualization,
methodological detail, and the overall discussion in the revised manuscript. We also appreciate the
continued engagement and thoughtful critique. Regarding the two core issues mentioned as being
incompletely addressed, we have revisited these concerns carefully in this revision. Below, we provide
a detailed explanation of how we have further clarified and expanded on these points in the manuscript.
Major comments:
1. Limited scope of studies- The authors offer a compelling description of how their current work makes
use of historic control RM studies, explaining why data for many of the comparative conditions has
been previously published. They posit that it’s very important to understand the impact of simultaneous

Response: We thank the reviewer for making this important point. We have now added text to this effect
both in the Introduction (lines 88-91) and Discussion (lines 391-401). Regarding the exclusion of
controls, the authors believe that the science is well established on that issue, with multiple labs
including ours (e.g. PMID: 21781131, PMID: 27601645, PMID: 31479428) as well as Joanne Flynn’s,
Philana Lin’s, showing extensive reactivation due to SIV co-infection in macaques with prior, controlled
Mtb infection. As a result, we did not include macaques in the untreated groups in order to reduce the
total number of macaques assigned to the project. It would be virtually impossible, to get an IACUC
protocol approved at a Primate Center, with uninfected macaques undergoing procedures as a control
group, as the justification to have these animals undergo procedures is not going to be accepted.
2. Limited information gleaned from the scRNAseq experiment: The authors engaged additional
expertise in scRNAseq analysis, which improved the technical analysis and visualization of the work.
However, there’s still no biological interpretation, take-away, or implication offered for the scRNAseq
data, which makes it hard to understand what these experiments and figures add to the overall
narrative.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback regarding the biological interpretation of our scRNA-
seq data. In response, we would like to clarify the biological insights derived from this analysis and how
they contribute to the overall narrative of our study.
To understand the lung-compartment–specific immune dynamics during Mtb/SIV co-infection and
treatment, we conducted longitudinal single-cell transcriptomic profiling of BAL cells at four critical
stages in the same animals. This design allowed us to monitor immune shifts within individual animals,
avoiding the need for separate control groups.
Our analysis revealed a clear immunological signature associated with SIV co-infection, including a
significant reduction in the presence of CD4+ T cells (which is highly expected) as well as NK/NKT
cells, with a concomitant increase in CD8+ T cells, macrophages, and monocytes. These shifts reflect
hallmark features of HIV-induced immune dysregulation and demonstrate the lung-specific impact of
co-infection. Importantly, these alterations were not reversed by cART+3HP, indicating persistent
immune dysregulation despite treatment.
Further, differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses revealed robust activation of
innate immune pathways—particularly type I IFN responses—following SIV co-infection. These findings
suggest that type I IFN signaling plays a central role in modulating the local immune environment in the
lung during co-infection. Moreover, changes in expression of TH1-, TH17-, and immune activation–
related genes across cell subsets underscore the functional remodeling of host immunity over time.
In summary, our scRNA-seq data provide critical biological insights into the temporal evolution of
immune responses during Mtb/SIV co-infection and treatment. The enrichment of interferon and innate
immune pathways supports the concept that immune activation, rather than restoration of protective
immunity, may dominate in the lung despite therapy. These findings offer mechanistic context to our
broader conclusions and highlight potential therapeutic targets for improving outcomes in TB/HIV co-
infection.
As will be seen below in response to other questions, we have significantly enhanced both the quantity
and quality of scRNAseq analyses through our collaborators at UT Houston Department of
Bioinformatics and Biostatistics.
